These notes go with the [τ ≈ 1 sweet-spot cartoon](index.qmd). The notes cover what
the cartoon deliberately simplifies, the physics needed to answer the questions
a careful student is likely to ask, and some discussion questions.

Background: Section III.C of N. Jeevanjee, "Climate sensitivity from
radiative-convective equilibrium: A chalkboard approach," *Am. J. Phys.*
**91**, 731–745 (2023), <https://doi.org/10.1119/5.0135727>.

## The idea

At a single wavelength, how much a layer sends to space is the product of two
competing factors. Deeper layers contain more absorbers, and by Kirchhoff's law
they therefore emit more. But a photon from deeper down must cross more
absorbers to get out. High up, nearly every photon escapes, but there are few
emitters. Deep down there are many emitters, but almost nothing escapes. The
product peaks where the optical depth to space is $\tau \approx 1$.

## What the cartoon simplifies

**1. The sweet spot exists only per unit height.** In the paper's model for
CO₂ (its Eq. 20), $\tau \propto p^2$: the $p^2$ comes from the absorber column
above (one factor of $p$) and pressure broadening of the absorption lines
(another factor of $p$). With $p \propto e^{-z/H}$ this gives
$\tau \propto e^{-2z/H}$, so every $H/2 \approx 3.75\;\text{km}$ of height
changes $\tau$ by a factor of $e$. A slab of thickness $dz$ therefore sends to
space an amount proportional to

$$\left|\frac{d\tau}{dz}\right| e^{-\tau} \;\propto\; \tau\, e^{-\tau},$$

which peaks at $\tau = 1$. If you instead slice the column into layers of equal
$\Delta\tau$, each slice sends $e^{-\tau}\Delta\tau$, which is largest at the
top: no interior peak. The cartoon's comparison is fair because the thin layer
is drawn at least as tall as the $\tau \approx 1$ layer.

The thin region physically has no top, since $\tau \to 0$ only as $p \to 0$.
Truncating it at the dashed top-of-atmosphere (TOA) line is harmless. The whole
region above the level where the optical depth is $\tau$ contributes a fraction
$1 - e^{-\tau}$ of all the photons that reach space, which is finite however
tall the region is.

**2. At $\tau = 1$ itself, most photons are absorbed.** A photon emitted
straight up at $\tau = 1$ escapes with probability $e^{-1} \approx 37\%$. The cartoon's 5 of 8
is an average over the whole shaded layer. You can read the layer's optical
depth off the figure using the paper's interpretation of $\tau$ (its Eq. 17) as
total absorber cross-section divided by column area. Each glyph's width is
about 0.099 of the column width, so:

| Level | $\tau$ from glyph widths |
|---|---|
| top of shaded layer | 0.20 |
| bottom of shaded layer | 0.99 |
| surface | 3.7 |

The average escape probability across $\tau = 0.20$–$0.99$ is
$(e^{-0.20} - e^{-0.99})/0.79 \approx 57\%$, consistent with 5 of 8.

**3. The real peak is broad, and the top of the thick region contributes.** By
the same $e^{-\tau}$ weighting, the expected number of photons reaching space
from each region is:

| Region | Expected | Drawn |
|---|---|---|
| thin | 1.8 | 2 |
| $\tau \approx 1$ | 4.5 | 5 |
| thick | 3.5 | 0 |

The $\tau \approx 1$ layer still sends the most. Its lead over the thin layer is
drawn about right, 5 to 2 against an expected 4.5 to 1.8. The $\tau \approx 1$
layer's lead over the
thick region is much smaller than drawn: an expected 4.5 to 3.5, where the
drawing shows 5 to 0. The "every photon absorbed" rule describes the deep part of the thick
region; its top, just below $\tau = 1$, sends a sizable share to space. More
generally, $\tau e^{-\tau}$ falls to half its peak at $\tau \approx 0.23$ and
$\tau \approx 2.7$. The span between those two levels is about
$1.2H \approx 9\;\text{km}$, most of the troposphere.

**4. Emission is isotropic.** Molecules emit in all directions. The cartoon
shows only the upward photon from each.

**5. Absorbed energy is re-emitted at the local temperature.** An absorbed
photon's energy is thermalized by collisions, and the absorbing layer re-emits
at its own temperature. So each photon that reaches space was emitted at the
temperature of the layer it left, whatever path the energy took before that.
Re-emission at the local temperature is what ties the $\tau \approx 1$
level to the emission temperature $T_\text{em}$.

**6. The color-to-temperature order assumes temperature falls with height.**
That holds in the troposphere. The paper's model has an isothermal
stratosphere. In the real stratosphere temperature rises with height, so near
the center of the CO₂ band, at 15 μm, where $\tau \approx 1$ lies in the
stratosphere, the optically thin layer is *warmer* than the $\tau \approx 1$
layer. That is the narrow emission spike at the band center in observed
outgoing spectra.

**7. Not to scale.** The molecule counts (2, 8 and 27) and the layer heights
are illustrative. Each glyph is best read as a unit of absorbing cross-section
rather than a fixed number of molecules, because absorption per molecule grows
with pressure. If $\tau$ grew by the same factor across every layer as tall as
the $\tau \approx 1$ layer, as $\tau \propto e^{-2z/H}$ implies, the cartoon's 2
and 8 glyphs would set that factor at 4, and the thick region, two such layers
tall, would need $32 + 128 = 160$ glyphs, six times the 27 drawn.

## From photon counts to W/m²

The cartoon counts photons, but OLR weights each emitter by the Planck function
$B$ at its temperature: at one wavelength every photon has the same energy, and
a warmer emitter sends out more of them. In the troposphere, deeper layers are warmer,
so Planck weighting favors depth. It strengthens the $\tau \approx 1$ layer's
lead over the thin layer and narrows its lead over the thick layer.

The numbers below are my own estimates for an idealized all-troposphere column;
the paper does not give them. The estimates assume a wavelength of 14 μm, $T \approx 227\;\text{K}$,
a lapse rate of $6.5\;\text{K/km}$ and $H = 7.5\;\text{km}$.

- **How fast $B$ grows with depth:** $B$ rises about 2% per Kelvin, so it grows
  by a factor of $e$ every $\approx 7.6\;\text{km}$ of descent, or about
  $1.6\times$ per $H/2$ layer.
- **Why depth still loses:** transmittance $e^{-\tau}$, with
  $\tau \propto e^{-2z/H}$, falls double-exponentially with depth. A modest
  exponential increase in $B$ cannot offset that.

Relative to the $\tau \approx 1$ layer, for equal-height layers each a factor
of $e$ more opaque than the one above, with the energy computed from the
Planck function:

| Layer | $\tau$ range | Photons to space | W/m² to space |
|---|---|---|---|
| thin neighbor | 0.22–0.61 | 0.72 | 0.43 |
| $\tau \approx 1$ | 0.61–1.65 | 1 | 1 |
| thick neighbor | 1.65–4.48 | 0.51 | 0.76 |

With the approximation $B \propto \tau^\beta$, $\beta \approx 0.5$, the energy reaching space per
unit height goes as $\tau^{1+\beta} e^{-\tau}$. That peaks at $\tau \approx 1.5$,
about $1.5\;\text{km}$ below the $\tau = 1$ level. The contribution has a long
tail upward on the cold side. So the level whose temperature reproduces the
OLR, $\pi B(T_\text{em})$, sits higher, at
$\tau_\text{eff} = [\Gamma(1+\beta)]^{1/\beta} \approx 0.78$, where $\Gamma$
is the gamma function (the paper uses $\Gamma$ for the lapse rate). The exact
Planck function gives a peak at $\tau \approx 1.46$ and
$\tau_\text{eff} \approx 0.72$. The paper's $\tau = 1$ lies
between the peak and $\tau_\text{eff}$. In this column the $\tau = 1$ level is at
227 K and $T_\text{em}$ is 219 K, so placing all emission at $\tau = 1$
overestimates OLR at this wavelength by about 20%.

## Discussion questions

1. **Only some photons from the $\tau \approx 1$ layer escape, yet that layer
   sends the most to space. Why?** It has many more emitters than the thin
   layer. Its escape fraction is lower, but not low enough to cancel that
   advantage.
2. **Why compare layers of equal height rather than layers of equal optical
   thickness $\Delta\tau$?** See note 1. With equal-$\Delta\tau$ slices the
   topmost slice sends the most, so there is no sweet spot. Slices holding equal
   masses of CO₂ give a third answer: with $\tau \propto p^2$, each slice's
   emission to space goes as $\tau^{1/2} e^{-\tau}$, which peaks at
   $\tau = 0.5$.
3. **What happens to this picture if the CO₂ concentration doubles?** Every
   level's $\tau$ doubles, so the $\tau = 1$ level rises. Where temperature
   falls with height it is now colder and emits less, which is the route to
   radiative forcing.
4. **Why does the emitting layer's temperature matter for OLR in W/m², not
   just photon counts?**
   See the section on Planck weighting.
5. **At a wavelength where CO₂ absorbs more weakly, where does the sweet spot
   sit?** Lower and warmer. In the limit of very weak absorption it reaches the
   surface, and the atmosphere becomes transparent at that wavelength.

## Caption, alt text and credit line

Plain-text versions for pasting into a web page, slide notes or a learning
management system. They use Unicode τ so they survive outside LaTeX.

**Caption:**

> Why emission to space, per unit height, peaks near optical depth τ ≈ 1 (CO₂,
> one wavelength). Each molecule emits one photon straight up; the photon
> escapes unless a molecule lies directly above it. High up (τ ≪ 1, blue),
> every photon escapes but there are few emitters. Deep down (τ ≫ 1, red),
> there are many emitters but every photon is absorbed. In between (τ ≈ 1,
> purple), emitters are plentiful and many of their photons still escape, so
> this layer sends the most photons to space. Colors mark the emitting layer,
> from coldest (blue) to warmest (red).

The caption's "many" is deliberate. A photon emitted straight up from exactly
τ = 1 escapes with probability $e^{-1} \approx 37\%$; the cartoon's 5 of 8 is an average over a
layer spanning roughly τ ≈ 0.2–1 (see note 2 above).

**Short caption:**

> Emission to space per unit height peaks near τ ≈ 1: enough emitters, and
> enough of their photons still escape.

**Alt text:**

> Cartoon of an atmospheric column of CO₂ molecules in three layers, with more
> molecules lower down. Arrows show each molecule emitting a photon upward. Both
> photons from the sparse top layer cross the top of the atmosphere; five of
> eight from the shaded middle layer, labeled "τ ≈ 1, sweet spot", also escape;
> every photon from the dense bottom layer is absorbed by a molecule above it.
